b: This post is slightly outside the box (or outside the pie tin) because most people who batch prep meals or ingredients don't think to batch prep pie crusts. Yet why not?
This has been a cool season staple in my family's kitchen for a decade. Might as well share.

The post photo is a lemon meringue pie fresh from the oven. The backyard lemons were basically free and the eggs were purchased on a $0.99/dozen special. Will be using the leftover egg yolks to bake a blueberry custard pie tonight.
Savory dinner pies often take just 5 minutes to prepare the filling, if only the crust weren't an issue. That's where batch prepped crust is useful.
Winters in my home include a steady rotation of quiches, pot pies, and cottage pie/shepherd's pie.

Prebake the crust while mixing ingredients, then fill the crust and bake until the top turns golden brown. We usually make single serving quiches because I adore mushrooms and the better half doesn't.

We'll change up the filling based on what's on hand. It's a wholesome meal that needs less than 10 minutes of hands-on attention. We'll use up post-Thanksgiving turkey as quiches or pot pies depending on that month's price of eggs.
It's also handy to have premade crusts at home when fresh filling ingredients come into seasonal sale, such as sweet potatoes at $0.99/lb, and when backyard pie fruits are ready for harvest.

Assuming you already own a mixing bowl and at least one pie tin, there's a modest one time investment in basic equipment to make DIY pie dough. Price estimates are based on an Amazon search of current pricing.
$10 pastry mat + French rolling pin (sold as a set, could be purchased separately)

We've found that placing a dinner plate over rolled-out dough makes an adequate template for cutting a full size pie crust, and placing a tea saucer over dough makes an adequate template for sizing crust to our mini casserole dishes.

Most home cookbooks publish recipes for a single crust, which is a discouraging approach because it's a PITA to get out all the equipment and clean up separately for every baking session. Fortunately, pie crust dough can keep in the freezer for up to 3 months.

With what follows, my family bulk buys ingredients: flour in 50 lb bags, 4 lbs of butter at a time, etc. We follow market trends. (I'm the person who posted a heads-up to buy bulk flour last August). If you don't shop that way, you may be able to get similar bargains during holiday baking ingredient loss leader discounts.

The following recipe is adapted from my copy of The Professional Pastry Chef, Second Edition, by Bo Friberg. The original calls for bread flour and lard; have found from experience that all purpose flour and vegetable shortening are acceptable substitutions. Also, have researched US customary volume measurements for this post; am posting them alongside the original gram weight measurements.
455 g (2 cups/4 sticks) cold unsalted butter

Mix the dry ingredients first, then add butter and shortening and mix with the dough blender (it's a manual tool, not an electric blender). Sprinkle in ice water while blending until it achieves even consistency.

Then sift flour onto a pastry mat and onto the rolling pin, and flatten to an even thickness. The recipe recommends 1/8" thickness but I tend to roll my crusts slightly thicker for ease of handling. Chill in the refrigerator at least 30 minutes if using fresh.
For frozen storage, stack in layers while separating cut crusts with baking parchment. Store in a freezer safe Ziploc bag. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before using.

You could either roll out the cutting scraps into additional crusts, or else make pie toppings from them. For holiday gatherings, I'll add a dab of water to make the scraps hold together, roll them to crust thickness, and then use cookie cutters themed to the holiday. Add another dab of water on baking day to make cookie cutter pie top crust parts hold together, then brush with an egg wash before baking. On Thanksgiving, for instance, that becomes a pie topped with a medley of 'autumn leaves.' The presentation looks fancy and seems like more work than it is.
